'''Clark Edward Barwick''' (born January 9, 1980) is an American mathematician and [[Academic ranks in the United Kingdom|professor]] of pure mathematics at the [[University of Edinburgh]]. His research is centered around [[homotopy theory]], [[Algebraic K-theory|algebraic ''K''-theory]], [[higher category theory]], and related areas.

== Early life and education ==
Barwick grew up in [[North Carolina]], and in 2001 completed his [[Bachelor of Science|BS]] in mathematics at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/school-of-mathematics/people?person=589|title=Clark Barwick {{!}} School of Mathematics|website=www.maths.ed.ac.uk|language=en|access-date=2018-04-18}}</ref><ref name="Barwick 2018">{{Cite web|url=http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~cbarwick/papers/cv_public.pdf|title=Curriculum Vitæ of Clark Barwick|last=Barwick|first=Clark|access-date=2018-04-18}}</ref> Barwick was then a graduate student at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], and received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in mathematics in 2005 under the direction of Tony Pantev.

== Career ==
Barwick held [[Postdoctoral Fellow|postdoctoral fellowships]] at the [[University of Göttingen|Mathematisches Institut Göttingen]] (2005–2006) and at the [[University of Oslo|Matematisk Institutt, Universitetet i Oslo]] (2006–2007).<ref name="Barwick 2018" /> Barwick spent the year 2007–2008 at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], and from 2008–2010 was a [[Benjamin Peirce]] Lecturer at [[Harvard University|Harvard]]. In 2010 Barwick became an [[assistant professor]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], and in 2013 he became the Cecil and Ida Green Career Development Assistant Professor of Mathematics. In 2015 Barwick was a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright]] visiting professor at the [[University of Glasgow]] and was promoted to Cecil and Ida Green Career Development [[Associate professor|Associate Professor]] of Mathematics at MIT, a position which he held until he became a reader at the University of Edinburgh in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.glasgowheart.org/schools/mathematicsstatistics/about/studentstaff/newsletterarchive/october15/headline_425779_en.html|title=University of Glasgow – Schools – School of Mathematics & Statistics – About us – Information for current students and staff – Newsletter Archive – October 15 – Meet Fulbright Professor Clark Barwick|website=www.glasgowheart.org|language=en|access-date=2018-04-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180421030858/http://www.glasgowheart.org/schools/mathematicsstatistics/about/studentstaff/newsletterarchive/october15/headline_425779_en.html|archive-date=2018-04-21|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://188.65.115.112/about/meet-our-fulbrighters/clark-barwick/1111|title=US-UK Fulbright Commission|website=188.65.115.112|language=en|access-date=2018-04-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180421062335/http://188.65.115.112/about/meet-our-fulbrighters/clark-barwick/1111|archive-date=2018-04-21|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2020, Barwick was promoted to a professor at the University of Edinburgh.<ref>The University of Edinburgh Senatus Academicus, 27 May 2020. [https://www.ed.ac.uk/files/atoms/files/20200527agendapapers.pdf www.ed.ac.uk/files/atoms/files/20200527agendapapers.pdf]. Retrieved 2021-03-03</ref>

== Research and notable works ==
A theme in Barwick's work is the homotopy theory of higher categories. In his early career, he frequently collaborated with [[Daniel Kan|Dan Kan]]; much of their work was concerned with models for the homotopy theory of homotopy theories. In his joint work with Chris Schommer-Pries, Barwick proved a unicity theorem for the homotopy theory of [[(∞, n)-category|(∞,''n'')-categories]].

Barwick has also made contributions to algebraic ''K''-theory. In particular, Barwick defined higher-categorical generalizations of [[Waldhausen category|Waldhausen categories]] and Waldhausen's [[S-construction|''S''-construction]] and used these to extend [[Friedhelm Waldhausen|Waldhausen's]] ''K''-theory to the setting of [[Quasi-category|(∞,1)-categories]]. Using this new theory, he proved the Theorem of the Heart for Waldhausen ''K''-theory. In joint work with [[:no:John Rognes|John Rognes]], he generalized [[Daniel Quillen|Quillen's]] [[Q-construction|''Q''-construction]] to the higher-categorical setting, providing higher-categorical generalizations of [[Quillen's theorems A and B|Quillen's Theorem B]] as well as Quillen's dévissage argument in the process. Much of his recent work has concerned [[Equivariant algebraic K-theory|equivariant algebraic ''K''-theory]] and [[Equivariant algebraic topoloy|equivariant homotopy theory]]. Barwick won the 2019 [[Berwick Prize]] of the [[London Mathematical Society]] for his paper "On the algebraic ''K''-theory of higher categories" where he "proves that Waldhausen's algebraic K-theory is the universal homology theory for ∞-categories, and uses this universality to reprove the major fundamental theorems of the subject in this new context."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lms.ac.uk/news-entry/28062019-1621/lms-prize-winners-2019|title=LMS Prize Winners 2019 – London Mathematical Society |author= | language=en |date=2019-06-28 |access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1112/jtopol/jtv042| title = On the algebraic ''K''-theory of higher categories| journal = [[Journal of Topology]]| volume = 9| issue = 1| pages = 245–347| year = 2016| last1 = Barwick | first1 = Clark | mr = 3465850| arxiv = 1204.3607| s2cid = 119160499}}</ref>

In 2019 Barwick with his student Haine introduced the theory of [[pyknotic object]]s. Which was published coincidentally and  is very closely related to that of [[Condensed mathematics|condensed sets]], with the main differences being set-theoretic in nature: pyknotic theory depends on a choice of [[Grothendieck universe]]s, whereas condensed mathematics can be developed strictly within [[ZFC]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/pyknotic+set|title=Pyknotic sets|website=nLab}}</ref>
